5. To leap or spring: a horse "leaps" under the warrior's sword (Job 39:23), it is a dry and energetic movement, a burst of vital energy.
H7493.origine: The verb comes from a Hebrew root that first describes a movement of shaking or vibration. The family of the word designates everything that trembles, oscillates, stirs: the central idea is that of a momentary or lasting instability. The word applies to both the physical world (the earth, mountains) and the political world (kingdoms).
H7493.emploi: This verb appears about 30 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the Psalms, the prophets, and vision narratives. In the Psalms (Psalms 18:8, 46:4, 68:9, 77:19), to tremble describes the earth reacting to thunder or the anger of God. In the prophets—especially Isaiah, Jeremiah, and Ezekiel—the trembling becomes a sign of divine judgment: kingdoms, nations, and strongholds tremble before punishment (Isaiah 14:16; Jeremiah 49:21; Ezekiel 26:15). In Haggai (2:6, 2:7, 2:21), it describes the shaking of creatures before the arrival of the Messiah. A unique occurrence: Job 39:23 speaks of the horse that "leaps" under the sword, another meaning of the same root.
H7493.portee: This word reminds the believer that nothing on earth is truly stable: only God is unchanging. In the face of powers that seem unshakeable—kingdoms, idols, riches—the Bible proclaims that they tremble under the gaze of the Lord. It is a word of comfort for the weak and a warning for the proud: whoever puts their hope in God will not be shaken (Psalms 46), while everything that stands without him will eventually falter.

sens: Agitation, noise of a great physical commotion
Earthquake, shaking of the ground
Trembling of a person, tremor of the body
Noise or vibration of an object in rapid motion
H7494.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes an intense noise accompanied by physical agitation: it is the tumult of an army on the march, the crash of a massive movement. In Jeremiah 47:3, it is the "noise" of the hooves of horses and the rumbling of chariots that creates this overwhelming tumult.
2. It often describes earthquakes, those shocks that shake the ground. When God passes before Elijah on the mountain (1 Kings 19:11), there is a "great earthquake," but the Lord is not in this spectacular manifestation.
3. The word also applies to the trembling of the human body, to fear or dread that shakes someone. It is an involuntary movement, the shockwave from the depths of one's being.
4. It can also evoke the whistling or quivering of a projectile in flight: in Job 41:20, the sea monster laughs "at the whistling of darts" that split the air, a sharp and vibrating noise.
H7494.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that evokes the idea of trembling, agitating, vibrating. Words of the same family refer to violent or disorderly movements. It is a concrete word that paints a physical reality: shaking, jolt, commotion. The Hebrew language loves words that speak to the body to evoke the great manifestations of God.
H7494.emploi: This word appears sixteen times in the Old Testament, mostly in the prophets (Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel). It describes sometimes impressive natural phenomena — earthquakes during divine interventions — and sometimes the human chaos of war or invasion. In 1 Kings 19, it paints the grand setting where God manifests to Elijah, but not in the tumult: it is precisely this contrast that stands out. In Ezekiel 37:7, when the dry bones gather by the prophetic word, there is a "movement" (the same word), a sign of life returning. The word covers both cosmic events and human reactions.
H7494.portee: This word reminds us that God is at work through the great upheavals of the world and history. But it also teaches, through the example of Elijah, that divine presence is not judged by the spectacular: the true God sometimes acts in silence, not in tumult. It is an invitation to seek God beyond strong emotions, and to recognize his hand even in the most terrifying movements of the world.

sens: Restore the physical health of a sick or injured person
Make again healthy or functional what is damaged (water, objects, wounds)
Restore the peace and prosperity of a nation or people
Forgive and restore the relationship with someone
Bring relief to inner or spiritual suffering
H7495.detail:
1. To heal primarily means to restore physical health: Abraham prays to God to heal Abimelech and his family (Genesis 20:17), or the injured servant receives care (Exodus 21:19). It is the action of the physician or God who removes the illness.
2. The word also applies to what is damaged or corrupted: healing a wound by bandaging it (Jeremiah 6:14), making bitter water drinkable (2 Kings 2:21), or cleansing a building afflicted by leprosy (Leviticus 14:48).
3. Healing can describe national restoration: God promises to heal the land if the people humble themselves and turn from evil (2 Chronicles 7:14). It is a healing of collective wounds.
4. In a deeper spiritual sense, healing means forgiving and reconciling: God heals, that is, forgives and restores, not only bodies but souls (Psalms 103:3). The psalmist asks God to heal him of his sin (Psalms 6:3).
5. Healing also carries the idea of consolation and comfort in the face of moral pain: the wound of Jerusalem is so grave that no one can heal it (Lamentations 2:13), and God heals the brokenhearted (Psalms 147:3).
H7495.origine: The Hebrew word rapa comes from a root that evokes the action of joining, connecting, putting together what is separated or broken. In Hebrew, the same family is found in words related to sewing or consolidation. The verb always emphasizes a return to a state of integrity. This root is found in several Semitic languages with the same sense of restoration. In the Greek translation of the Old Testament (the Septuagint), this Hebrew verb is rendered by the Greek iamai, which literally means "to bring from a bad condition to a good condition."
H7495.emploi: This verb is very frequent in the Old Testament: about 62 occurrences. It appears in all genres of texts — historical narratives (Genesis, 2 Kings), laws (Leviticus, Numbers), prayers and praises (Psalms), prophecies (Isaiah, Jeremiah), wisdom (Job). In the literal sense, healing mainly concerns diseases and wounds: leprosy lessons, Egyptian plagues (Deuteronomy 28:27), war wounds (2 Kings 8:29). In the figurative sense, the word extends to spiritual and national restoration: God heals the land, forgives sins, heals the wounds of the people. Jeremiah often uses this verb to describe the false consolation of lying prophets who "heal the wounds lightly" (Jeremiah 6:14; 8:11). The prophet Isaiah speaks of the sufferings of the Servant of the Lord: "By His stripes we are healed" (Isaiah 53:5), this verse announces a spiritual healing obtained through sacrificial suffering.
H7495.portee: This word reveals that healing, in the Bible, is never purely physical: it is always linked to God's mercy, forgiveness, and the restoration of the covenant. When the Christian prays for healing, he is not only asking for the end of symptoms but for the restoration of his integrity before God. The promise of Isaiah 53:5 announces that through the sacrificial death of Christ, our spiritual and eternal health is assured. Healing is therefore an act of divine love that touches the whole being.

sens: The spirits or images of the deceased in the afterlife
The inhabitants of the realm of the dead, the invisible underground world
Death itself, or the fate of the dead
What is weak, without substance, without reality
What is forgotten, annihilated, that does not return
H7496.detail:
1. The word designates the spirits of the dead, these vague and impalpable entities that inhabit the realm of the dead according to Hebrew conception. In Isaiah 14:9, the "shadows" of all the great ones of the earth are awakened, as if they retain a form of existence in the afterlife, albeit weakened and deaf to the praises of God.
2. These shadows collectively populate the underground kingdom: it is a collective of the deceased who form an assembly or community in the depths (Job 26:5, Isaiah 14:9). This place is often called the "realm of the dead" or "valleys of the realm of the dead."
3. Sometimes the word more broadly designates death itself or the mortal state, what becomes of the living who stray far from divine wisdom (Proverbs 21:16).
4. The shadows are compared to beings without power, without a strong voice: they do not rise to praise the living God (Psalms 88:11), unlike the living. They embody absence, emptiness.
5. The shadow of the dead is what disappears, is forgotten, does not return: in Isaiah 26:14, the dead do not come back to life, their shadows do not rise again.
H7496.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that evokes what is soft, weakened, without strength. The "shadows" are etymologically what remains of the dead: a vague image, without substance, without energy. This representation is typical of the Old Testament, where the deceased do not enjoy a happy life in a radiant afterlife, but exist as evanescent forms in the darkness of the realm of the dead. This is very different from the Christian promise of resurrection.
H7496.emploi: The word appears 8 times in the Old Testament, almost exclusively in the books of wisdom and the prophets (Job, Psalms, Proverbs, Isaiah). It always designates the spirits of the dead or the mortal condition itself. In Proverbs, it warns against the path that leads to the house of death: the strange woman "leans toward death" (2:18), and he who strays from wisdom "will rest in the assembly of the dead" (21:16). In Isaiah, notably 14:9, the shadows of kings are awakened to welcome the fallen king of Babylon, an image of power equalized by death. In Psalms 88:11, the context shows that the dead do not sing the praise of God, unlike the living.
H7496.portee: This word reminds the believer that death, in the Old Testament, is perceived as a diminishment, a shadow, an absence of true life before God. For the Christian of the New Testament, it opens the door to the resurrection and the eternal life promised by Christ. The contrast enriches our understanding of the divine plan: the Old Testament shows the limit of natural death, and the Gospel brings the hope of surpassing that limit.

sens: Ancestor of the Philistine giants during David's time
H7497A.detail: Rapha is the father or eponymous ancestor of a lineage of Philistine giants who confronted David and his warriors. His descendants — Ishbi-Benob, Saph, Lahmi, and others — were distinguished by their exceptional size and unusual physical traits, such as six fingers on each hand and foot. All these men perished in battles against David and his servants (2 Samuel 21:16-22; 1 Chronicles 20:6-8).
H7497A.origine: The name Rapha (רָפָה) is related to the Hebrew root that denotes healing or relief, but here it functions as a proper name of a house or clan of giants. The term "Rephaim" (רְפָאִים), which in Hebrew refers to the spirits of the dead or shadows, has been traditionally associated with the name of this giant, although the exact etymology remains debated. This proper name identifies a famous lineage in the accounts of David's wars.
H7497A.emploi: Rapha appears six times in the Bible, exclusively in the accounts of David's wars against the Philistines (2 Samuel 21 and 1 Chronicles 20). He is always presented as the ancestor of formidable warriors: Ishbi-Benob, Saph, and the man with six fingers from Gath. The Bible names him each time specifying that his descendants "were the children of Rapha" or "descendants of Rapha," thus highlighting a lineage of giants established among the Philistines. These passages show how David, although inferior in physical strength, defeated these men and theirs, marking the superiority of divine providence over brute military power.
H7497A.portee: The story of Rapha and his descendants reminds us that physical strength and impressive stature do not guarantee victory — only trust in God truly matters. The successive defeats of these giants by David illustrate a central theme of the Bible: God overturns the mighty and exalts the humble. For the Christian reader, this is an invitation not to fear seemingly invincible adversaries, but to place trust in the One who masters all earthly powers.

sens: Ancient people of giants who inhabited Canaan
Inhabitants of certain territories of Canaan and Transjordan
Region or land associated with this people
H7497B.detail:
1. The Rephaim are an ancient people known primarily for their impressive stature — they are giants. They are mentioned among the peoples that kings fought during Abraham's time: "Kedorlaomer and the kings who were with him […] defeated the Rephaim at Ashteroth-Karnaim" (Genesis 14:5). It is a formidable nation, established long before the arrival of the Israelites.
2. At the time of the conquest, some territories bear the name of this nearly extinct people, so closely is it linked to these places. Deuteronomy 2:11 notes that other peoples, such as the Moabites and Ammonites, also called giants from their own regions by this name, showing that the term designates a category of giants, not just a unique group. King Og of Bashan, who reigned during Moses' time, "was the last of the remnant of the Rephaim" (Deuteronomy 3:11), confirming that this people was fading away.
3. The region called "land of the Rephaim" (Deuteronomy 3:13) refers to the lands they once occupied, notably in Bashan and Gilead. These geographical names perpetuated the memory of a famous but vanished people.
H7497B.origine: The name Rephaim likely derives from a root meaning "giant" or "one who is great" in ancient Semitic languages. Several peoples of giants have different names — Anakim, Emim, Zamzummim — but all are sometimes referred to as Rephaim or compared to them. The reputation of this people was so established that its name became a generic term for giants in Canaan and neighboring regions.
H7497B.emploi: The Rephaim appear nine times in the Bible, primarily in the Pentateuch (Genesis and Deuteronomy) and in Joshua. They are first mentioned as a people that ancient kings fought (Genesis 14:5), then listed among the peoples from whom the Israelites would inherit the land (Genesis 15:20). The books of Deuteronomy emphasize their past: this people inhabited the lands east and west of the Jordan, but had largely disappeared or declined by the time of the conquest. Og of Bashan, the last known representative, was a formidable giant whose iron bed measured more than four meters (Deuteronomy 3:11). The word thus serves to evoke the antiquity of the Canaanite peoples and the power of the obstacles that the Israelites overcame by the strength of God.
H7497B.portee: The Rephaim remind the reader that God gave the Israelites a land where ancient and powerful peoples lived. Their disappearance or decline demonstrates the reality of the divine promise: God prepared the possession of Canaan by weakening those who occupied it. This reinforces confidence in God's faithfulness and power toward His people.

sens: Valley located near Jerusalem, between the Judean mountain and the coastal plain
Strategic territory where the Philistines established their camps
Region known to have belonged to an ancient population of giants
H7497G.detail:
1. The Valley of the Rephaim is a concrete valley, precisely located in the geography of Judah, near Jerusalem. It appears in the territorial delimitations of Joshua 15:8 and 18:16 as a geographical landmark for fixing the boundaries of the lands. It is a fertile valley, in a strategic area between the mountain and the plain.
2. This valley is the place where the Philistines, enemies of Israel, came to establish their camps and wage battle. In 2 Samuel 5:18 and 5:22, we see them "spreading out in the Valley of the Rephaim" during their attacks against David. It was thus an important battlefield during the wars between Israel and the Philistines.
3. The name itself recalls that this region once belonged to the Rephaim, an ancient population of giants. Although these giants had disappeared long before David's time, the valley retained their name, as a memory of the distant past of the land.
H7497G.origine: The word "Rephaim" derives from a Hebrew root meaning "the dead" or "the shadows" — it is interpreted as an allusion to these superhuman, almost ghostly beings who would have inhabited the land before Israel. In biblical tradition, the Rephaim designate an ancient race of giants, also mentioned in Genesis 14:5 and 15:20. The valley bears their name because it was one of their lands.
H7497G.emploi: The Valley of the Rephaim appears six times in the Bible, always in a territorial or military context. Three times in Joshua, it serves as a landmark to describe the boundaries of the territory of Benjamin and Judah. Four times in the accounts of David (2 Samuel 5, 23 and 1 Chronicles 11, 14), it is the place where the Philistines camp or gather to attack. It is always mentioned as a geographically significant place, linked to conflicts with the Philistine enemy or to the delimitations of the promised lands.
H7497G.portee: This valley reminds us that the promised land was not a peaceful gift: Israel had to conquer and defend it against powerful adversaries, such as the Philistines. The very name of the valley evokes an ancient past, populated by extraordinary creatures, showing that God masters history and lands, from distant ages to the present time.

sens: Ancestor of the Philistine giants
Family of large warriors who confronted Israel
H7497H.detail: 1. Rapha is the name of a man who lived during the time of the united monarchy in Israel, and from whom several renowned Philistine giants are descended. He is the father or ancestor of formidable warriors, notably Goliath, the most famous among them. 2. The term "children of Rapha" refers to a family of giants who fought against the warriors of Israel: in 1 Chronicles 20:4, Sippaï, one of these descendants, is mentioned as being killed by Sibbecaï during a battle at Gezer against the Philistines. These men were remarkable for their size and exceptional strength, making them formidable in battle.
H7497H.origine: Rapha comes from a root meaning "to heal" or "to relax," but the precise meaning of the name remains obscure. What is certain is that Rapha has become the eponymous name of a lineage of giant warriors, probably a princely family or dynasty among the Philistines. The descendants are referred to as "Raphides" or "children of Rapha" to indicate their belonging to this clan of giants.
H7497H.emploi: Rapha appears only once in the Segond 1910, in 1 Chronicles 20:4, where he is mentioned as the ancestor of the giants encountered by the troops of the king of Israel. Although the text does not provide biographical details about Rapha himself, it informs us that his descendants produced several giant warriors who confronted Israel at different times. These battles between the giants of Rapha and the men of Israel constitute a remarkable part of the historical narratives of the Bible.
H7497H.portee: The memory of Rapha and his descendants reminds us that the history of God's people has been marked by confrontations against powers that seemed humanly invincible. These giants represent, for Israel, obstacles that could only be overcome by the power of God. The fact that these giants were ultimately defeated by the warriors of Israel testifies to God's faithfulness to His people.

sens: Man of the tribe of Benjamin
H7498G.detail: Rapha is a man of the tribe of Benjamin, mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 8:37. He is the son of Binea and the brother of Eleasa and Atsel. He belongs to the genealogical lineage of Saul, the first king of Israel, and lived during the time of the divided monarchy, after the schism between Judah and Israel.
H7498G.origine: His name means "tall" in Hebrew. He is also known by the name Rephaiah in 1 Chronicles 9:43, a variant of the same name. He comes from an important family of Benjamin, descended from Saul through his genealogy.
H7498G.emploi: Rapha appears only once in the biblical genealogies, in 1 Chronicles 8:37, in the list of descendants of Saul. He is also mentioned in 1 Chronicles 9:43 under the name Rephaiah. These genealogical lists serve to establish the origins of the families of the people of Israel and to show the continuity of the royal lineage after the fall of the house of Saul.

sens: Son of Benjamin mentioned in the genealogy of the people of Israel
H7498H.detail: Rapha is a son of Benjamin, first mentioned during the enumeration of the sons of Benjamin who went down to Egypt with Jacob (Genesis 46:21). His name reappears in the genealogical list of 1 Chronicles 8:2, where he is presented as the fifth son of Benjamin. He is the brother of Bela, Becher, Ashbel, Gera, Naaman, Ehi, Muppim, Huppim, Ard, and Jediael. Although not detailed in the biblical narratives, he represents one of the founding branches of the tribe of Benjamin.
H7498H.origine: The name Rapha (רָפָא) means "great" or "tall," possibly reflecting a physical characteristic of the one who bore it. It is a Hebrew name that belongs to the patriarchal period and the early days of the Israelite people, serving to identify the ancestors of the chosen people.
H7498H.emploi: Rapha appears only once in the Segond 1910 translations: in 1 Chronicles 8:2, where he is listed as the fifth son of Benjamin. This mention is part of a genealogical list that reconstructs the descendants of Benjamin after the return of the people. His discreet appearance shows that, although a member of the founding tribe of Israel, he did not play a major role in the historical or religious events reported in the Scriptures.

sens: concrete means to heal a wound or illness
medical treatment, care
solution to end an evil or calamity
H7499.detail:
1. The word primarily designates a physical remedy, a treatment to heal a wound or illness: it is the bandage, the balm, the intervention that heals. In Jeremiah 30:13, God tells Jerusalem that she has "no remedy, nor means of healing" — her wound is so grave that no care can heal it.
2. More broadly, it refers to anything used for healing: doctors use remedies, and Egypt, in Jeremiah 46:11, "multiplies remedies" but in vain, for its destruction is decided and irrevocable.
3. Figuratively, a remedy can also be a solution, a means to correct or stop a misfortune. When Pharaoh has a broken arm (Ezekiel 30:21) and he is not "bandaged to be healed," it means there are no resources to lift him up.
H7499.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root rafa, which means "to heal," "to repair." The feminine suffix -ah makes it an abstract noun: "the action of healing," then "that which heals." It is a word from a culture where the care of wounds was known (bandaging, balm) and where healing was understood as restoration, a return to health.
H7499.emploi: The word appears three times in the Hebrew Bible, always in the prophecies of Jeremiah and Ezekiel. It first describes concrete care: bandages, balm — what is used to treat a wound. But in each prophetic usage, the remedy is absent or ineffective, for God has decided on judgment. In Jeremiah 30:13 and 46:11, despite all the remedies in the world, Jerusalem and Egypt will not heal. It is a theological usage: the remedy becomes the measure of what is irredeemable. The image is that of a hopeless diagnosis.
H7499.portee: This word reminds us that healing, whether spiritual or physical, does not come from our own resources alone. When the Bible speaks of the absence of a remedy, it invites the reader to recognize that some evils — notably the judgment of God — cannot be circumvented by our efforts. But conversely, it affirms that God is the true healer, and that all genuine care comes from Him.
